newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian cyclone to hit coast by Wednesday evening.
newsitem.headline: Indian cyclone to hit coast by Wednesday evening.

text.p: A powerful cyclone has slowed its advance towards India's southeastern state of Andhra Pradesh and could cross the coast later on Wednesday, giving residents more time than expected to prepare for the storm.

Officials said the cyclone, which was earlier expected to hit Andhra Pradesh around noon, was likely to strike the coast later in the evening. "The storm's advance seems to have slowed down. It is likely to hit land only by evening," J.V.M Naidu, director of the cyclone warning centre at Visakhapatnam port, told Reuters.
"It is quite worrying that it is slowing down...it seems to be intensifying further," he said. "We are not certain when it will hit land, but it will be later in the day."
At 11.30 a.m. local time (0600 GMT), the storm was 150 km (93 miles) southeast of Machilipatnam port in the Bay of Bengal and was moving in a west-northwesterly direction, he said.
Naidu said the storm was expected to cross the coast between the towns of Ongole and Kakinada.

Officials said they expected the storm to whip up winds of 150-180 kmh (94-113 miles per hour) and tidal waves of two to three metres high (six to nine feet) which are expected to flood low-lying coastal areas up to 10 km (six miles) inland.
A Kakinada resident reported rain and a heavily overcast sky. Residents sought shelter indoors and there was little activity in the streets.
State authorities said they had evacuated people from low-lying areas anticipating severe flooding. About 150,000 people had been moved to relief camps, they said.
Rail and road services were suspended and power switched off in areas likely to be affected by the cyclone.
The cyclone, the second in a month, was expected to cause widespread damage.

Coastal areas in Andhra Pradesh were devastated by a November storm that left more than 2,000 people dead or missing at sea. It damaged crops and property worth more than 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion).
Officials fear the latest cyclone may cause more damage than the last. Areas limping back to normal after the last storm may once again face the hurricane's fury.
Traffic along the east coast between Vijayawada town and Madras, capital of neighbouring Tamil Nadu state, was expected to be crippled.

"Train traffic, which has just resumed between Vijayawada and Madras, might collapse again under the fresh onslaught," said Naidu. "The overhead electric traction wires will snap and we expect large sections of rail track to be washed away."
Power and telecommunications cables could snap, causing a total loss of electricity supply and communications, he added.
